Optimization of micro-aeration intensity in acidogenic reactor
of a two-phase anaerobic digester treating food waste
Suyun Xu a,b, Ammaiyappan Selvam b, Jonathan W.C. Wong b,⇑
a Department of Environmental & Low-Carbon Science, School of Environment and Architecture, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, China
b Sino-Forest Applied Research Centre for Pearl River Delta Environment, Department of Biology, Hong Kong Baptist University, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 12 February 2013
Accepted 28 October 2013
Available online 27 November 2013
Keywords:
Micro-aeration
Acetic acid
Butyric acid
Methane production
Protein hydrolysis
a b s t r a c t
Micro-aeration is known to promote the activities of hydrolytic exo-enzymes and used as a strategy to
improve the hydrolysis of particulate substrate. The effect of different micro-aeration rates, 0, 129,
258, and 387 L-air/kg TS/d (denoted as LBR-AN, LBR-6h, LBR-3h and LBR-2h, respectively) on the solubi-
lization of food waste was evaluated at 35 C in four leach bed reactors (LBR) coupled with methanogenic
upﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactor. Results indicate that the intensity of micro-aeration
inﬂuenced the hydrolysis and methane yield. Adequate micro-aeration intensity in LBR-3h and LBR-2h
signiﬁcantly enhanced the carbohydrate and protein hydrolysis by 21–27% and 38–64% respectively.
Due to the accelerated acidogenesis, more than 3-fold of acetic acid and butyric acid were produced in
LBR-3h as compared to the anaerobic treatment LBR-AN resulting in the maximum methane yield of
0.27 L CH4/g VSadded in the UASB. The performance of LBR-6h with inadequate aeration was similar to that
of LBR-AN with a comparable hydrolysis degree. Nevertheless, higher aeration intensity in LBR-2h was
also unfavorable for methane yield due to signiﬁcant biomass generation and CO2 respiration of up to
18.5% and 32.8% of the total soluble hydrolysate, respectively. To conclude, appropriate micro-aeration
rate can promote the hydrolysis of solid organic waste and methane yield without undesirable carbon
loss and an aeration intensity of 258 L-air/kg TS/d is recommended for acidogenic LBR treating food
waste.

1. Introduction
During the acidogenic phase of an anaerobic digestion, a large
consortium of microorganisms that are capable of solubilizing or-
ganic substrates such as carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, work
together and produce organic acids (i.e., lactic, acetic, butyric and
propionic acids, etc.). Among the organic acids produced, butyric
acid (HBu) and acetic acid (HAc) are known to be better precursors
of methane production (Yang et al., 2003; Montero et al., 2010),
especially HAc, which is regarded as the most important product,
contributing 65–95% of methane production (Weber et al., 1984);
in contrast lactic acid can seriously inhibit hydrolysis and metha-
nogenesis (Zhang et al., 2007; Li et al., 2008). Therefore, conversion
of organic matters into HAc and HBu in the hydrolytic-acidogenic
stage will improve the overall energy yield (Yang et al., 2003)
and increase the process rate. Techniques employed to enhance
the solubilization of organic substrates into volatile fatty acids
(VFAs) include pH control (Yu and Fang, 2003; Cysneiros et al.,
2008), addition of enzymes/microbes (Cirne et al., 2008) and phys-
icochemical/thermal pretreatments (Hartmann and Ahring, 2006).
In the recent studies, several authors documented the advan-
tage of incorporating micro-aeration in the hydrolytic-acidogenic
reactors for solubilizing the sludge and other organic substrates.
Jagadabhi et al. (2010) found that the production of VFAs from
the leach bed reactor (LBR) fed with energy crops increased from
2.2 to 9.0 g/L by the application of micro-aeration at 1 L/min. Zhu
et al. (2009) demonstrated that the hydrolysis rate was improved
by 30.9–57.7% with the provision of sufﬁcient micro-aeration re-
gime of 5 min aeration in every 4 h at a ﬂow rate of 0.7 L/min as
compared
with
those
treatments
with
insufﬁcient
aeration
(5 min/24 h) and complete anaerobic conditions. In contrast,
Nguyen et al. (2007) reported that the hydrolysis rate of municipal
solid waste was not improved with the aeration for 2 h at 1 L/min
after 4 h interval; however, a positive effect on the performance of
methanogenic phase was observed.
Although, these studies have compared the micro-aeration
intensity and effectiveness in the hydrolysis of various organic sub-
strates, the relationship between micro-aeration and acidiﬁcation
rate has not been completely understood in terms of the extent
and types of VFAs produced in LBR. Furthermore, the composition

of VFAs would affect the performance of subsequent methanogenic
reactor. Despite the reported advantages of micro-aeration, the
residual oxygen in the acidogenic leachate from LBR may inhibit
the activity of methane-forming bacteria and decrease the meth-
ane yield. Therefore, the objective of the present study was to
study the effect of different intermittent micro-aeration rates on
the solubilization and speciation of VFAs in the anaerobic hydro-
lytic-acidogenic LBR reactor coupled with an up-ﬂow anaerobic
sludge blanket (UASB) reactor. Material balance based on metabo-
lites and by-products distribution in the LBR and the methane pro-
duction in the UASB of the two-stage LBR-UASB system was used
as the reference for the selection of optimum micro-aeration
intensity.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Anaerobic digesters and materials
Four identical sets of laboratory scale LBR-UASB systems were
used for the experiments. The working volume of acidogenic LBR
and methanogenic UASB were 4.6 L and 10.0 L respectively. The de-
tailed conﬁgurations of reactors were presented in our previous re-
port (Xu et al., 2011). Synthetic food waste (FW) with a total solids
(TS) content of 38.5 ± 1.0% with volatile solids (VS) content of
97.1 ± 0.2% (VS/TS) was used as the substrate (Wong et al., 2009).
Anaerobically digested sludge (ADS) collected from the Shek Wu
Hui wastewater treatment plant, Hong Kong, with 5.2% TS and
86.1% VS/TS was used as the inoculum for acidogenic reactor.
2.2. Experimental design
Experiments were performed for a total of 17 days at 35 C with
two replicates for each treatment to obtain reproducible results.
Intermittent micro-aeration was applied using an air pump con-
nected to the bottom of the LBRs with a ﬂow rate of 1.0 L/min;
and the operation was controlled using timers. Four micro-aeration
frequencies were evaluated, i.e., aeration for 12 min every 6 h
(LBR-6h), 3 h (LBR-3h), 2 h (LBR-2h) and no aeration (LBR-AN)
resulting in corresponding micro-aeration rates of 129, 258, 387
and 0 L-air/kg TS/d, respectively.
Each LBR was initially packed with a mixture of 1.0 kg FW and
0.2 kg of anaerobically digested sludge (ADS). Additionally, 10%
wood chips (in volume basis) were added as the bulking agent to
facilitate the liquid leaching (Xu et al., 2011). Then 1.0 L of tap
water was added into each LBR on Day 0. Leaching occurred natu-
rally and the leachate was collected at the bottom of the reactors
daily. Half of the collected leachate was diluted with equal volume
of tap water and adjusted to pH 6.0 using sodium carbonate before
recycling back into the LBR. The remaining half of the collected
leachate was fed into the UASB reactor for methanogenesis.
2.3. Analytical methods
The volume of biogas produced from the UASB reactor was
measured using a wet gas ﬂow meter (BSD-0.5, Shanghai, China)
and concentration of methane in the biogas generated was deter-
mined using a gas chromatograph (GC-HP7890) equipped with a
thermal conductivity detector. Total solids (TS) and volatile solids
(VS) content of the FW and seed sludge were determined by oven
drying at 105 C for 24 h and igniting at 550 C for 16 h in a mufﬂe
furnace, respectively. Total organic carbon (TOC) content of the FW
and digestate were determined by dichromate oxidation method
(Nelson and Sommer, 1982). The total Kjeldhal nitrogen (TKN)
content of the FW and digestate were determined by digestion
and spectrophotometric determination of ammonium-nitrogen
(NH4
+-N) according to the APHA Standard Method 4500-Norg C
(APHA, 2005).
Acidogenic leachate from the LBR and methanogenic leachate
from the UASB reactor were collected everyday and analyzed.
The pH and ORP were measured with a pH/ORP meter (Orion
920, Thermo). The concentration of chemical oxygen demand
(COD), NH4
+-N and TKN were analyzed according to the Standard
Methods 5220C, 4500-Norg C and 4500-NH3 F, respectively (APHA,
2005). For the analysis of VFAs, leachates were ﬁltered through
0.45 lm cellulose acetate membrane ﬁlter paper and 0.9 mL was
transferred to GC vials with the addition of 0.1 mL formic acid.
The concentrations of acetic acid, propionic acid, n-butyric acid,
iso-butyric acid, n-valeric acid and iso-valeric acid were deter-
mined using a HP 6890 Series gas chromatograph (Hewlett Pack-
ard) equipped with ﬂame ionization detector and Econo-Cap
EC1000 (15 m  0.53 mm  1.20 lm) column. The sample injec-
tion volume was 1 lL. The temperatures of the injector and detec-
tor were maintained at 200 C and 250 C, respectively, while the
column temperature was programmed with an initial temperature
of 120 C for 5 min, increasing to 160 C at a rate of 5 C/min, and
holding at 160 C for 5 min to ensure complete VFAs volatilization.
The sum of acetic acid, propionic acid, n-butyric acid, iso-butyric
acid, n-valeric acid and iso-valeric acid concentrations are reported
as total VFAs (tVFA).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Performance of LBRs with varied micro-aeration intensities
3.1.1. Changes in pH, ORP and volume of leachate
Recycling of acidogenic leachate back to LBR and adjusting the
pH of the recycling leachate to 6.0 enhanced the hydrolysis as
shown in our previous study (Xu et al., 2011). Therefore, 50% of
the acidogenic leachate was mixed with equal volume of tap water,
adjusted the pH using sodium carbonate and then recycled back to
the LBR in order to recycle part of the hydrolytic enzymes and re-
duce the acid crisis. The volume of leachate produced in LBR ran-
ged from 480 to 520 mL for most of the period (Fig. 1a), and the
differences in decomposition rate among the four treatments inﬂu-
enced the percolating property resulting in varied levels of leach-
ate production.
The pH of LBRs ranged from 3.8 to 4.2 in the ﬁrst 3 days, and
then gradually increased. During the whole digestion process, pH
of LBRs’ leachate that was recycled to LBR was daily adjusted to
6.0, thus the pH ﬂuctuated around 6.0. The pH in four LBRs was
approaching the range of 5.5–6.5 after about one week of digestion.
At the beginning of digestion, ORP of digestate was around 56 mV
and decreased gradually along the digestion period. By the end of
digestion, ORP decreased to the level between 200 mV and
300 mV. The ORP values showed a contrasting proﬁle to that of
the pH proﬁle as reported by Zhu et al. (2009). ORP is negatively
associated with pH if only the half reaction [H+]/[H2] is accounted.
In LBRs with micro-aeration, ORP increased to 125–215 mV on the
second day and then decreased immediately to the level between
150 mV and 300 mV in the following one week, whereas ORP
in LBR-AN decreased gradually right at the beginning of digestion.
The initial increase followed by a rapid decrease of ORP can be
attributed to the stimulation of facultative microorganisms, which
leads to the accelerated consumption of oxidants. Nevertheless, the
ORP level in LBR-2h was higher than others indicating compara-
tively higher level of oxidants in this reactor.
3.1.2. Changes in COD, TKN and NH4
+-N contents of leachate
As presented in Fig. 2a, COD concentrations of the ﬁrst day
digestion ranged from 7.9 to 9.3 g/L, which was followed by the

peak values observed on the second or third day, i.e. COD concen-
trations of 41.8, 61.3, 43.5 and 49.4 g/L, respectively, for LBR-AN,
6 h, 3 h and 2 h. The relatively low concentration of soluble hydro-
lysate in leachate indicates that the stagnation period of hydrolysis
was about one day. A similar pattern was found for TKN and
NH4
+-N leaching also. However, the trend varied among four treat-
ments. COD concentration in LBR-3h exhibited the peak of 61.3 g/L
on the second day and the highest levels ranged 25.4–30.8 g/L
during the subsequent digestion period. Concentration of COD in
LBR-AN reached the maximum value of 49.4 g/L on the third day
and maintained the second highest level during the latter phase;
while LBR-2h and LBR-6h ranked the third and fourth. Similar
trend was found for TKN also as presented in Fig. 2b. TKN concen-
trations of LBR-3h were in the range of 660–1252 mg/L, while
LBR-2h and LBR-6hranged between 200 and 878 mg/L.
During the initial stage of digestion, difference in NH4
+-N con-
centrations among the four treatments was insigniﬁcant, but there
was a distinct increase in LBR-3h in the late period of digestion
indicating that the aeration intensity may exert effects on the
deamination or related nitrogen transformation. The tradeoff be-
tween the higher protein decomposition rate of 70.8% (Table 2)
and the lower concentrations of TKN and NH4
+-N as detected in
leachate from LBR-2h, indicates that some soluble NH4
+-N might
have escaped from the reactor as ammonia with air ﬂushing, or
part of the nitrogen might have transformed into nitrate/nitrite
through aerobic nitriﬁcation. Since the hypothesis of ammonia
emission through air ﬂushing is not supported by the fact that
the pH level in LBRs was lower than 6.5, which is not favorable
for ammonia volatilization, nitriﬁcation could be the major factor,
but additional studies are required to conﬁrm this reasoning.
3.2. VFAs production and speciation in acidogenic LBRs
3.2.1. VFAs production
As shown in Fig. 3, at the beginning of digestion, no signiﬁcant
differences in the tVFA concentrations were found among four
LBRs, which indicate that the performance of LBR at the early stage
was mainly inﬂuenced by the inoculum-born microbial activity. On
the second day of digestion, nearly 3-fold higher concentration of
tVFA was observed in LBRs with micro-aeration than that of con-
trol (LBR-AN). Afterwards, concentrations of tVFA in LBR-AN was
the lowest throughout the digestion process. As shown in Fig. 3f,
the speciﬁc yields of VFAs in LBR-AN was 0.09 g COD/g VSadded,
which was lower than LBR-6h, 3h and 2h (0.26, 0.40 and 0.18 g
COD/g VSadded, respectively). A positive effect of micro-aeration
on the VFAs production was also reported by Jagadabhi et al.
(2010) using grass-silage as substrate. Limited oxygen concentra-
tion would result in the accumulation of reduced organic matter
due to the poor tricarboxylic acid cycle (Jensen and Michelsen,
1992). Tiquia et al. (1996) also found that regulated limitation of
oxygen could result in the accumulation of fermentative metabolic
products under facultative environment. Thus the application of
micro-aeration could enhance the acid fermentation and promote
the production of VFAs compared with anaerobic treatment. Fur-
thermore, the optimum ORP range for acid fermentation was
known to be 100250 mV. As seen in Fig. 1c, ORP level in
LBR-AN was higher than 100 mV before Day 7, whereas ORP in
other three LBRs decreased to lower than 100 mV from Day 4,
which may lead to the lower level of tVFA in LBR-AN.
Nevertheless, tVFA levels in LBR-6h, 3h and 2h were inﬂuenced
by different aeration intensities. The highest tVFA level of 17.5–
21.8 g COD/L was observed in LBR-3h during the period of Day 6
to 17. In case of LBR-6h, the concentrations of tVFA peaked on
Day 4 (18.3 g COD/L) but decreased gradually to 6.23 g COD/L by
the end of operation. Furthermore, tVFA level in LBR-2h was much
lower than LBR-6h and LBR-3h, indicating the negative effects of
higher levels of aeration. Johansen and Bakke (2006) also observed
that the accumulation of VFAs in the digester with micro-aeration
of 15 s per min was only half of the anaerobic reactor. These

bic bacteria and aerobic respiration leading to the lower level of
intermediate products. Thus more VFAs were generated in LBR-
3h with a comparatively low aeration rate, while more VFAs were

3.2.2. VFAs speciation
HAc and HBu were the two main species of VFAs produced in all
LBRs as seen in Fig. 3a and b. This result is consistent with the pre-
vious reports of Han and Shin (2004) and Komemoto et al. (2009)
using FW as the substrate. In present study, the pH values of four
LBRs were in the range of 4.5–6.5, which would be favorable for
the acidogenesis. Solubilization of carbohydrates increase substan-
tially and results in an increase in the generation of all acids when
pH increases to >4.5; whereas, when the pH increases to >6.5, HBu
production essentially ceases (Fang and Liu, 2002). Since the pH of
LBRs was below 6.5 in this experiment, HBu was produced all
through the experiment in consistent with the earlier reports. Dur-
ing the initial 5 days of digestion, HAc predominated in all LBRs,

Meanwhile, the ratios of tVFA/COD in the ﬁrst day ranged from
21% to 53%, which were relatively low compared to the values of
73–98% at the end of digestion (Fig. 3e). This is probably due to
the contribution of formic acid and lactic acid, which were re-
ported to account for 50% of the total soluble products (Zhu
et al., 2009). Therefore, although the formic acid and lactic acid
were not analyzed in this study, it can be reasonably assumed that
these species may contribute to the remaining COD.
After Day 5, the production of HAc was reduced while the
productions of HBu and propionic acid (HPr) were increased corre-
spondingly. HAc constituted about 31.3–43.8% of tVFA produced in
the Control during the period of Day 8–17; whereas, only 9.8–
17.5%, 3.3–16.4% and 6.7–30.7% of HAc were observed in LBRs with
aeration intensities of 12 min/6 h, 3 h and 2 h, respectively. As
summarized in Table 1, the fraction of HPr increased from 3% of
tVFA in LBR-AN to 12%, 7% and 5% in LBR-6h, 3h and 2h, respec-
tively; the production of HVa also increased from 2% of tVFA in
LBR-AN to 3–11% in LBRs with micro-aeration. Conclusively,

micro-aeration accelerated the fermentation as well as shifted
the metabolism from HAc production to HBu and HPr production.
The decomposition of easily degradable carbohydrates is reported
to be associated with the production of HAc, while the hardly
degradable carbohydrates increase the production of HPr (Lü
et al., 2009).
HAc and HBu are the desirable VFAs in the acidogenic phase of
anaerobic digestion to maximize methane production (Yang et al.,
2003). In contrast, accumulations of HPr and HVa would be limit-
ing factors for methane generation. In the present study, although
the proportions of HPr and HVa were increased in reactors with
aeration, the production of HAc and HBu were also increased
due to the higher yield of tVFA. Micro-aeration intensity of
258 L-air/kg TS/d in LBR-3h increased the production of VFAs;
furthermore, the summed content of HAc and HBu was at a
comparable level (90%) as compared to LBR-AN (95%). Neverthe-
less, the absolute content of HAc increased signiﬁcantly from
0.06 of LBR-AN to 0.23 g COD/g VSadded of LBR-3h, which could
be favorable for methane generation.
3.3. Overall performance of LBR-UASB System
The hydrolysis rate and methane yield of FW under different
micro-aeration intensities are presented in Table 2. The degree of
hydrolysis for each treatment is calculated based on the VS re-
moval, while the decomposition efﬁciencies of carbohydrate and
protein are calculated according to the TOC and TKN removal. De-
grees of hydrolysis in LBR-3h and LBR-2h were 66.3% and
78.1%respectively, showing improvement when compared with
the control LBR-AN (61.2%). Furthermore, carbohydrate and pro-
tein hydrolysis efﬁciency were enhanced from 65.4% and 43.2%
in LBR-AN to 70.8% and 78.1% in LBR-2h. The positive impacts of
micro-aeration on the hydrolysis efﬁciency of carbohydrates and
protein have been reported by several researchers (Hasegawa
et al., 2000; Jagadabhi et al., 2010; Lim and Wang, 2013). Hasegawa
et al. (2000) also reported that the hydrolysis rate and methane
yield from sewage sludge was improved by 50% after micro-
aeration treatment. The improved hydrolysis could be attributed
to the stimulation of fermentative bacteria to excrete hydrolytic
enzymes (Nguyen et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2009). In the anaerobic
fermentation of organic waste, the facultative bacteria can con-
sume oxygen and induce anaerobic conditions, while the strict
anaerobes supply metabolites for facultative bacteria (Ueno et al.,
2006; Li and Fang, 2007). Thus, regulating the intermittent aeration
or micro-aeration could stimulate the effective co-existence of fac-
ultative bacteria and anaerobes (Sang et al., 2009). However, the
protein decomposition (42.7%) and degree of hydrolysis (60.1%)
in LBR-6h were comparable with the control LBR-AN; probably re-
lated to the unstable enzyme activity under the insufﬁcient aera-
tion (Zhu et al., 2009). Furthermore, the soluble hydrolysate
contents as indicated by the speciﬁc COD yield did not correlate
positively in all the treatments. LBR-3h with an intermediate aera-
tion rate produced the highest speciﬁc COD yield of 0.78 g COD/g
VSadded, while the insufﬁcient aeration in LBR-6h and excess aera-
tion in LBR-2h resulted in lower COD yields of 0.45 and 0.52 g COD/
g VSadded, as compared to the control (0.58 gCOD/g VSadded). With a
decrease in intermediate soluble products, the ﬁnal methane yields
in the UASB decreased correspondingly. As shown in Table 2, the
highest methane yield of 0.27 L CH4/g VSadded was achieved with
LBR-3h and the lowest yield of 0.17 L CH4/g VSadded was observed
for LBR-6h; and this trend reﬂects the speciﬁc COD production in
the LBR.
The optimum micro-aeration intensity of 258 L-air/kg TS/d in
the present experiment was comparable to the study of Zhu
et al. (2009) with sufﬁcient aeration intensities of 147 and 442
L-air/kg TS/d. However, these values were much higher than that
reported by Johansen and Bakke (2006), and Lim and Wang
(2013), which were about 33 L air/kg TS/d and 57 L air/kg TS/d. This
difference might be related to the way of intermittent aeration ap-
plied in Zhu et al. (2009) and in the present study, while continu-
ous micro-aeration with a low ﬂow rate was applied in other two
references. In our study, 12 L of air passed through LBR during each
time of ventilation, nevertheless it is difﬁcult to completely con-
sume this volume of oxygen within 12 min. Therefore the practical
oxygen supply should be much less. The micro-aeration intensity
of our study was estimated to be 16, 32 and 48 L air/kg TS/d
according to the working volume of reactor. Then the micro-aera-
tion intensities among above studies are comparable. Furthermore,
oxygen supply in micro-aeration treatments ranged from 12% to
35% of feed COD, which was comparable to 16% reported by
Botheju et al. (2010).
3.4. Carbon balance based on metabolites and by-products distribution
Hydrolysis breaks down the particulate substrate into soluble
substrates such as sugars; and the extracellular enzymes play a
crucial role in the hydrolysis. Subsequently, the hydrolyzed partic-
ulate substrates (SHy) are utilized by the acidogens, to produce
VFAs and gases (CO2 and H2). The total amount of SHy,TOC can be ex-
pressed based on the carbon balance according to the following
equation,
SHy;TOC ¼ XBm;TOC þ SIn;TOC þ BiogasTOC
ð1Þ
where SIn,TOC is the soluble intermediate products in the efﬂuent
from acidogenic reactor on the basis of TOC, XBm,TOC is the biomass
proliferation using hydrolyzed substrate. SHy,TOC is calculated from
the discrepancy of TOC content between the initial and ﬁnal

The hydrolyzed nitrogenous organic matters (SHy,N) is distrib-
uted in the soluble intermediate products containing nitrogen
(SIn,N) and the biomass generation (XBm,N) as expressed in the fol-
lowing equation,
SHy;N ¼ XBm;N þ SIn;N ¼ ðN=CÞXBm  XBm þ ðN=CÞSIn  SIn
ð2Þ
where (N/C)XBm and (N/C)SIn are the nitrogen to carbon ratio of bio-
mass and intermediate products, respectively. SHy,N is calculated
from the difference of TKN content in digestate before and after
digestion, while SIn,N is the cumulative TKN content eluted in the
leachate. Thus XBm,N can be evaluated according to Eq. (2), and a
typical biomass composition (CH1.8O0.5N0.2) was referred to calcu-
late the content of XBm as suggested by Johansen and Bakke
(2006). The distributions of residual substrate (SRe), hydrolyzed sub-
strate (SHy), soluble intermediate products (SIn), biogas and biomass
(XBm) in LBRs are shown in Fig. 4a. In the succeeding methanogenic
stage of digestion, acetotrophic methanogens and hydrogenotroph-
ic methanogens make use of VFAs, CO2 and H2 to produce methane.
However, a part of organic matters are also used for biomass gener-
ation or ﬂow out with efﬂuent. The ratio of methane production to
the inﬂuent SIn,N in each treatment is presented in Fig. 4b.
As illustrated in Fig. 4a, SRe decreased with the increasing micro-
aeration rate, and SHy increased correspondingly from 65.5% in
LBR-AN to 83.0% in LBR-2h. However, the SIn did not follow the
same trend as that of the total hydrolysis rate. With an intermedi-
ate aeration rate, the SIn of LBR-3h accounted for 75.7% of the total
amount of SHy and it gave the maximum COD yield correspond-
ingly. When aeration rate increased to 12 min/2 h, the SIn only ac-
counted for 48.7% of SHy. Similarly, the carbon loss due to
respiration under excess micro-aeration has also been reported
by Charles et al. (2009) and Jenicek et al. (2008) with the substrate
of organic solid wastes. Moreover, the increased biomass genera-
tion was found in LBRs with the higher aeration rate. As shown
in Fig. 4a, LBR-2h showed the highest yield of bacterial growth of
18.5% (XBm/CODhydrolyzed), while LBR-AN, LBR-6h and LBR-3h had
much lower levels of 0.9, 6.6 and 3.3%, respectively. Akutsu et al.
(2009) found that the yield of bacterial growth tended to decrease
with an increase in the total concentration of undissociated organic
acids and attributed this phenomenon to the decreased availability
of ATP. This explained why the biomass generation in LBR-3hwas
much lower than that of LBR-2h. Therefore, the tradeoff between
the high hydrolytic efﬁciency and the lower level of organics being
available for methanogenesis should not be neglected, because the

In the methanogenic reactor, the efﬁciency of transforming SIn
into CH4 was quite similar in all four treatments, in the range of
54.6–60.5% (Fig. 4b). Thus, the methane yield in UASB was posi-
tively correlated to the amount of SIn obtained in acidogenic LBR.
The highest methane yield of 0.27 L CH4/g VSadded was achieved
in UASB connected to LBR-3h with the highest COD concentration
in leachate.
4. Conclusions
This study evaluated the effects of four micro-aeration intensi-
ties on the hydrolysis and methane yield of food waste in a two-
phase anaerobic digester. The optimum micro-aeration intensity
was 258 L-air/kg TS/d in LBR-3h that accelerated COD leaching
and enhanced methane production by 5% and 18%, respectively.
The generation of HAc and HBu in LBR-3h was more than three
times higher than the treatment with anaerobic treatment LBR-
AN resulting in the maximum methane yield of 0.27 L CH4/g
VSadded. The performance of LBR-6h with inadequate aeration
was similar to LBR-AN with a comparable hydrolysis rate and de-
creased methane yield. Nevertheless, higher aeration intensity in
LBR-2h was also unfavorable for methane yield due to the oxida-
tion of intermediate soluble products, which decreased the speciﬁc
COD production to 0.19 L CH4/g VSadded although with a high de-
gree of hydrolysis. Results indicate that optimal rate of micro-aer-
ation can promote the solubilization of solid organic waste without
undesirable carbon loss and the aeration of 258 L-air/kg TS/d is
advantageous for food waste.
